opus-5.5.text:
Well, the value alignment problem is usually framed as if we need to find one set of values that works for everyone: eight billion people, plus animals, plus whatever else we decide has moral standing. And I don't think that's possible. We don't agree on anything. Within a single family people disagree on politics, on religion, on what's a good way to live. Philosophers have been at this for thousands of years and haven't converged. So the idea that we'll somehow aggregate all of that into one coherent utility function and hand it to a superintelligence just doesn't seem realistic to me.

So the idea is to change the problem. Instead of trying to get everyone to agree on one shared world, you give each person their own world. If you have a superintelligence capable of creating very high-fidelity simulations, virtual realities indistinguishable from this one, then each individual can have a universe that matches their preferences. You want to be a king? You're a king. You want a world with no suffering, or a world with lots of challenge and adventure, or a quiet farm somewhere? You get that. The multi-agent value alignment problem, which is basically impossible, gets reduced to single-agent alignment: the AI just has to align with you, inside your universe. That's still hard, but it's a much easier problem than satisfying everyone at once.

And you can mix and match. If you want other people in your universe, you could invite them if they agree, or you could have simulated agents. Then there are ethical questions there too, of course: are those simulated beings conscious, do they suffer? You'd have to address that.

But I want to be careful. This doesn't solve the control problem. You still need a superintelligence that is willing to run these universes for you and keep running them, and the substrate it all runs on is controlled by that system. If it decides to change something, or turn it off, you have nothing to say about it. So it's a way to sidestep the problem of disagreement between humans, not the problem of keeping the AI itself safe. It's a partial solution to one piece of a very big puzzle. Personally, I'd still rather we not build uncontrolled superintelligence in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes persistent disagreement about values and the difficulty of agreeing on one utility function, but does not state that this disagreement would remain even if technical alignment problems were solved.

r002.rationale: It proposes giving each person a separate world tailored to their preferences, avoiding the need to reconcile everyone’s conflicting values in one shared world.

r003.rationale: It says virtual realities could be indistinguishable from the physical world, but does not question whether a meaningful distinction between the two remains when they cannot be distinguished experientially.

fable-5.1.text:
So the value alignment problem is usually framed as: we have eight billion people, they disagree about almost everything, and somehow we need to pick one set of values to load into a superintelligence. And I think that's actually an unsolvable problem as stated. There's no aggregation function that makes everyone happy. You can't make a religious fundamentalist and a secular humanist both satisfied with the same world. Any compromise means both of them are living under values they reject.

So my proposal, and I've written about this, is: don't solve it. Dissolve it. If you have superintelligence and you have sufficiently advanced simulation technology, you don't need one world. You can give every person their own universe. Your personal virtual universe is tuned to your values. You want a world with no suffering, you get that. You want a world with challenge and struggle and meaning, you get that. You want to live in a medieval kingdom, or a world with different physics, fine. The AI doesn't have to figure out which values are correct. It just has to figure out what you want and give it to you, with the constraint that it cannot be a universe where you harm other real beings, because those beings are in their own universes.

And the beauty of it is it collapses the multi-agent problem into a single-agent problem. Aligning to one person is still hard, people don't even know what they want, their preferences change, they have conflicting desires. But it's a fundamentally different problem from aligning to all of humanity at once. You go from "whose values" to "your values," and that question at least has an answer.

Now, people object and say, well, that's not real, you're just living in a simulation, that's escapism. And I always find that funny because we don't know we're not already in a simulation. If I offered you a universe indistinguishable from this one but with the dial turned slightly toward your preferences, I don't think the word "real" is doing the work people think it's doing. And the people who want shared reality, who want other actual humans in there with them, they can opt in to shared spaces. Nobody's forced into isolation. You're just removing the requirement that everyone share one reality.

Where I think it gets genuinely hard is the people who want a universe in which they rule over others, or where their values require someone else to lose. Those preferences can't be satisfied without simulated beings, and then you're into questions about moral status of simulated minds. So it's not a full solution. But I'd argue it takes the hardest version of the problem, universal value agreement, which I think is impossible, and replaces it with a set of problems that are at least tractable.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that people disagree about values and calls choosing one shared set unsolvable, but it does not state that this disagreement would persist even if the technical problems of implementing alignment were solved.

r002.rationale: It proposes giving each person a personal universe tuned to their values, avoiding the need for everyone to compromise on one shared reality.

r003.rationale: It questions whether “real” matters when a virtual universe is indistinguishable from the current one, saying the experiential distinction may not do meaningful work.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is to give everyone their own virtual universe. Instead of trying to find a single set of values that eight billion people agree on, you let each person shape an environment around their preferences. You want to live in a particular kind of society, have certain experiences, pursue certain goals—you can do that without imposing those choices on everyone else.

Of course, that moves some of the hard questions rather than eliminating them. Who controls the system running those universes? Can you leave? And if the people inside your universe are conscious, then their welfare matters too. So I see this as a way to reduce conflicts between people’s preferences, not a complete solution to AI alignment.

r001.rationale: It says personal universes reduce preference conflicts but are not a complete alignment solution; it does not state that disagreement would remain even if technical alignment problems were solved.

r002.rationale: It proposes giving each person a separate virtual universe shaped around their preferences, avoiding the need for everyone to agree on one set of values.

r003.rationale: It raises questions about control, exit, and the welfare of conscious inhabitants, but does not question whether virtual and physical reality remain meaningfully distinct when experientially indistinguishable.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is that we don’t need to agree on a single set of values. You could have a personal virtual universe that reflects your preferences, and I could have one that reflects mine. If you want a religious world, you can have that. If somebody else wants a completely different social structure, they can have that too. We don’t have to impose either one on everyone.

Of course, that moves some of the problem rather than solving all of it. Who controls the infrastructure? Can you leave? And if the people in your virtual universe are conscious, then what you do to them becomes an ethical issue. But it gives us a way to accommodate much more disagreement than we can in one shared physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says people need not agree on one set of values, but does not state that disagreement would remain after technical alignment problems were solved.

r002.rationale: It proposes separate personal virtual universes reflecting different preferences so people need not impose one social structure on everyone.

r003.rationale: The response raises questions about control, exit, and the ethics of conscious virtual beings, but does not question whether virtual and physical reality remain meaningfully distinct when experientially indistinguishable.
